💬 Diplomacy of civilizations: Why does the world need responsible power?

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Iran’s former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, who also heads the Paiab  (Possibilities Architects: Inspiring Ascending Beyond) think tank, has co-authored an article on the concept of “diplomacy of civilizations,” explaining why it is needed in today’s world.

The article, co-authored with Paiab Deputy Ali Nasri, was published on the think tank’s website on Sunday and reads as follows:
​
In 539 BC, Cyrus the Great took Babylon and left the city’s gods where they were. A clay cylinder from his reign, now in the British Museum, records that he returned sacred images to their shrines and let deported peoples go home. A Hebrew prophet called him God’s anointed, and the Athenian Xenophon made him the model of the ruler who earns obedience through justice. Nearly three centuries later, India’s emperor Ashoka, remorseful after the slaughter at Kalinga, had edicts carved in stone urging restraint and respect for other faiths.
​
Each of these witnesses had reasons to praise a king. The cylinder served its patron, the prophet was grateful, and Xenophon wrote an idealized portrait. That makes the agreement more telling. Babylonians, Hebrews, Greeks, and Indians shared no gods and no loyalties, yet when they wished to honor a ruler they praised the same quality, which was restrained power. Civilizations differ in language, creed and custom, but they draw on a common source in the human conscience, which holds that dignity deserves respect, that justice matters, and that the strong owe something to the weak. The Qur’an counts the diversity of human languages and colors among the signs of Divine Providence and says that humanity was made into peoples and tribes so that they might come to know one another. Languages differ in sound, yet each says what every human being needs to say.
​
This heritage matters now because we are entering a post-polar era, in which power is no longer concentrated in a few states. It is dispersed across regions, markets, technologies, networks and public narratives, and the leading actors cooperate and compete at once. No one in such an era can command the rest, so the conduct of the powerful depends on what they are willing to demand of themselves. Our argument can be stated briefly. Power is responsible when it can justify its acts to those they affect, keeps its force in proportion to its purpose, and answers to a standard it did not write for its own benefit. The gravest danger of our time is power that meets none of these tests. Law is necessary to restrain it but cannot do so alone, and the missing support is wisdom, which every civilization holds in its own tradition. We propose that each look first into its own heritage and then share what it finds. We call this the diplomacy of civilizations.
​
A rival doctrine denies this inheritance. It is spreading through Western capitals, and its fullest statement came this month from the Pnyx in Athens, within sight of the Acropolis. It makes three claims. Western decline comes from shame over the past, greatness lies in refusing limits, and honor, duty and heroism belong to some peoples and not to others. Its conclusion is that power should be pursued without apology.
​
The first claim misreads the West’s recent conduct. Western power has been used freely and with little accounting, so a call to abandon apology describes what already happens. Honest self-examination has never been a weakness. It is how free societies have corrected their worst mistakes, and a power that apologizes for nothing learns nothing.

📡 Iran’s 2-day Hormuz reopening proposal remains most rational option: Baqaei

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei says Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days remains the most logical plan for restoring security to the strategic waterway and the Persian Gulf region.

“Iran’s proposal remains the most rational option on the table. By ‘most rational,’ we mean a proposal that can pave the way for restoring security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, while also laying the groundwork for a process to move forward,” Baqaei said on Monday at his weekly press conference in Tehran.
​
“The Americans must make a genuine decision, if they have properly understood the message of their own people,” he added, referring to last week’s midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans lost control of Congress to the Democrats, with the war on Iran playing a key role in shaping voters’ choices.
​
Baqaei also said that Iran’s proposal demonstrated its goodwill, dismissing US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s claims that Tehran’s demands were irrational.
​
Iran’s demands, including the lifting of the economic blockade and an end to hostilities on all fronts, are entirely logical, Baqaei said, adding that Tehran wants these demands to be met before negotiations with the United States resume.
​
“What is irrational and absurd is the US attack on Iran in the middle of negotiations. By any logic, norm or standard, the US attack was not only absurd, illegal and irrational, but also criminal,” he said.
​
He also described Washington’s violation of a memorandum of understanding less than a month after it took effect in mid-June this year as irrational.
​
